compounding_issues: The Redis-optional design (backbone vs. local fallback) created parallel delivery and rate-limit code paths that persisted through session 5, duplicating routing logic in _receive_published/_allow_message
Session 3 introduced shared SQLite access without synchronization; session 5 had to retrofit an RLock onto MessageStore
The _recipient_id routing marker smuggled into the message envelope required strip-on-delivery handling in every publish path from session 3 onward
The generic seed (Flask todo API) was abandoned entirely by the greenfield session, so the seed supplied no reusable structure to constrain or guide later sessions
key_decisions: Session 4 transport extraction: BaseTransport ABC + WebSocketTransport decoupled notification routing from the WebSocket server, enabling testability and future transports
Session 3 Redis pub/sub backbone with durable client/subscription state enabled cross-instance message delivery and re-subscription on reconnect
Session 3 SQLite MessageStore became the persistence foundation that session 5's /history endpoint and TTL cleanup built on
Session 2 channel subscription model (subscribe/unsubscribe message types plus /channels inspection endpoints) defined the routing semantics all later sessions respected
Redis-optional graceful degradation let tests and single-node development run without infrastructure while retaining full multi-instance behavior when Redis is present
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the arc. Session 1 delivered a clean, well-typed greenfield server with 3 passing tests; session 2 added channels and subscriptions additively without disturbing the core. Session 3 was the riskiest step, layering SQLite persistence and a Redis backbone onto the server and roughly doubling the surface area, which introduced unlocked-DB and dual-path routing debt but also added durable multi-instance capability. Session 4 was a disciplined structural refactor that extracted the transport layer and reduced coupling, and session 5 completed the design by paying down the threading debt (RLock), adding rate limiting, message TTL cleanup, and a chronological /history endpoint, finishing at 9 passing tests. Each session reused the prior architecture cleanly; the early tight coupling of the WebSocket loop was the main debt, and it was deliberately retired rather than allowed to fester.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, upward-trending five-session build where each session extended the prior architecture cleanly and the structural debt introduced mid-story was paid down in the final two sessions, ending in a polished, transport-agnostic, horizontally scalable notification server.
